cards.text: The LORD gives a statute to Moses, Israel's leader, and Aaron, his brother and Israel's priest (Exodus 4:14; 28:1). The Israelites are to bring an unblemished red heifer that has no defect and has never been placed under a yoke. It goes to Eleazar the priest, Aaron's son (Exodus 6:23), who has it brought outside the camp and slaughtered in his presence.

Eleazar takes some of its blood on his finger and sprinkles it seven times toward the front of the Tent of Meeting. Then the heifer is burned in his sight: its hide, its flesh, its blood and its dung. The priest throws cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet wool onto the burning heifer.
Now everybody who worked this job cleans up. The priest washes his clothes and bathes before he comes back into the camp, and the man who burned the heifer washes and bathes too.

cards.question: The priest and the man who burned the heifer have both washed their clothes and bathed. True or false: they're still ceremonially unclean until evening.

cards.text: No amount of scrubbing changes it. It's like my oven timer. I can stare. I can pace. I can BEG. That batch is done when the timer says it's done.
Then a man who is ceremonially clean gathers up the ashes and stores them in a clean place outside the camp. Israel holds on to those ashes the way I hold on to my last bag of chocolate chips.

cards.question: The congregation keeps the heifer's ashes for preparing the water of ___.
The LORD says what the water of purification made from the heifer's ashes is for. Purification from what?
The man who gathered up the heifer's ashes was ceremonially clean when he started. True or false: he's still clean once he's gathered them.

cards.text: So he washes his clothes and stays unclean until evening, just like the other two. Three men. Three loads of laundry. ONE heifer. The LORD calls this a permanent statute for the Israelites and for the foreigner residing among them.
Now the statute turns to the people who will need those ashes. Whoever touches any dead body is unclean for seven days and must purify himself with the water on the third day and on the seventh day.

cards.question: Someone touches a human corpse and never purifies himself. True or false: he defiles the tabernacle of the LORD.

cards.text: That person must be cut off from Israel. His uncleanness is still on him, because the water of purification has not been sprinkled on him.

When someone dies in a tent, everyone who enters and everyone already inside is unclean for seven days. Any open container in there without a lid fastened on it is unclean too. Out in the open field, anyone who touches someone killed by the sword or who died of natural causes, or a human bone, or a grave, is unclean for seven days.

Here's where those stored-up ashes come in. Some go into a jar, with fresh water poured over them. Then a man who is ceremonially clean dips hyssop in the water and sprinkles the tent, its furnishings and the people who were there, plus anyone who touched a bone, a grave or a person who died or was slain.

cards.question: The clean man sprinkles the unclean person on the third day and on the seventh day. True or false: right after the seventh day's sprinkling, that person is clean.

cards.text: First the one being cleansed washes his clothes and bathes in water, and that evening he's clean. But if an unclean person does not purify himself, he's cut off from the assembly, because he has defiled the sanctuary of the LORD.

The one who sprinkles the water of purification must wash his clothes, and whoever touches that water is unclean until evening. So the man getting everybody clean has some cleaning up of his own to do, like scrubbing the whole kitchen and ending up the messiest thing in it.

cards.question: One last rule: anything the unclean person touches becomes ___.

cards.text: And anyone who touches that thing is unclean until evening. That's the whole statute, friend, start to finish.
